content: Taribavirin, also known as viramidine and codenamed ICN 3142, is an antiviral medication currently undergoing Phase III clinical trials. It has not yet been approved for pharmaceutical use. This drug is a prodrug of ribavirin, meaning it is metabolized into ribavirin in the body, and it exhibits activity against a variety of DNA and RNA viruses. One of the distinguishing features of taribavirin is its improved liver-targeting properties compared to ribavirin. It has a shorter half-life in the body due to reduced penetration into and storage within red blood cells. This characteristic makes it a promising candidate for the treatment of viral hepatitis syndromes where ribavirin is effective, such as hepatitis C, and potentially hepatitis B and yellow fever. In preclinical animal models, taribavirin has demonstrated antiviral activity against influenza that is comparable to ribavirin, but with slightly reduced toxicity. This suggests that taribavirin may eventually replace ribavirin as a preferred treatment for influenza as well. The drug is being developed by Valeant Pharmaceuticals International, which is the parent company of Ribapharm. Ribapharm was the first to report the synthesis and testing of taribavirin in 1973. Currently, Valeant is focusing on evaluating taribavirin as a treatment for chronic hepatitis C. From a chemical perspective, taribavirin contains a carboxamidine group, which is somewhat basic. As a result, the drug is often administered as its hydrochloride salt form, which has a distinct chemical formula and identifiers (such as ChemID and PubChem numbers). At physiological pH, the carboxamidine group undergoes partial protonation, resulting in a positive charge on the molecule. This charge slows the drug's ability to cross cell membranes, such as those of red blood cells, until it is metabolized into ribavirin. In the liver, taribavirin undergoes first-pass metabolism, during which the carboxamidine group is converted into a carboxamide group. This transformation enhances the concentration of ribavirin in liver cells and bile when taribavirin is administered, contributing to its targeted action in hepatic tissues.
